notes.b: A region is an area of the earth's surface that shares one or more characteristics, called criteria, which make it different from the areas around it.
points: Physical criteria: climate, relief and rock type.
Administrative criteria: the boundaries set by government.
Cultural criteria: language and religion.
Socio-economic criteria: wealth, employment and development.
Urban criteria: a city and its hinterland.
These five types of region are the five subsections of this chapter.

Regions exist at different scales. A local region is a county or a city's hinterland, e.g. Co. Clare; a national region is the West of Ireland; a continental region is North West Europe; a global region is the Islamic world.

A single index defines a region by one criterion: rock type alone gives a karst region. Multiple indices combine several criteria: a peripheral region can be defined by income, unemployment and out-migration together.
Physical and cultural regions usually merge into their neighbours through transition zones rather than ending at a sharp line.
Administrative regions have exact boundaries, fixed by law.
Regions also change over time as their criteria change.

notes.b: A climatic region is a large area with similar temperature, precipitation and seasonal pattern, usually with similar natural vegetation and soils.
points: The world can be divided into climatic regions. This subsection studies the cool temperate oceanic type in detail.
Cool temperate oceanic: Ireland and North West Europe.
Warm temperate oceanic: the Mediterranean type, with hot, dry summers and mild, wet winters.
Hot desert: e.g. the Sahara.

notes.h: Characteristics of the cool temperate oceanic climate
points: Mild winters: mean January (coldest month) temperatures are about 4–7°C.
Cool summers: mean July (warmest month) temperatures are about 14–16°C.
Small annual range of temperature, only about 10°C; snow is rare on low ground.
Rain falls in every month, so there is no dry season.
Changeable weather, with prevailing south-westerly winds.
Latitude: Ireland lies between about 51.5°N and 55.5°N, in the mid-latitudes, where the sun's angle is moderate.
North Atlantic Drift: a warm ocean current, the extension of the Gulf Stream, keeps winters mild and coasts free of ice.
Maritime influence: the sea heats and cools slowly, so the annual temperature range is small.
Prevailing south-westerly winds blow off the Atlantic, carrying its mild, moist air over Ireland.
Frequent Atlantic depressions and their fronts bring rain. These weather systems are taught in geo-weather-climate.
Relief rainfall: moist air is forced up the western mountains, cools and releases its rain on their western slopes.
The west is wetter than the east: about 1,000–1,250 mm of rain a year across much of the west, against about 750 mm in the driest parts of the east, around Dublin.
Over 2,000 mm a year falls on many western mountains.
The east lies in a rain shadow, sheltered from the south-westerly winds by the western uplands.
Wet days (days with measurable rain): about 150 a year on the east and south-east coasts, rising to about 225 a year in parts of the west.
The south-east is the sunniest region.
The north is slightly cooler than the south, and coasts are milder in winter than the inland Midlands.

notes.h: North West Europe and the eastward transition
points: The international setting: the same climate covers Ireland, Britain, north-west France (Brittany), Belgium, the Netherlands, Denmark and coastal Norway.
All of these face the Atlantic, share the North Atlantic Drift and lie in the path of westerly depressions.
Moving east, away from the Atlantic, winters become colder, summers warmer, the annual range larger and rainfall lower, with a summer maximum. This is the continental influence.
The change is gradual, so the boundary of a climatic region is a transition zone, not a line.

notes.h: Climate and the region's other features
points: Natural vegetation is deciduous forest, mainly oak and ash.
Soils are brown earth.
Grass grows for most of the year, which favours pastoral farming in Ireland, mainly cattle and dairying.

notes.b: A geomorphological region is an area with a distinctive landscape produced by the same rock type, geological structure or landforming processes.
The Burren in north-west Co. Clare is a karst region on Carboniferous limestone. Formation of its landforms is taught in geo-rocks-weathering-s4; here each landform is only named.
points: The name comes from the Irish Boireann, meaning rocky place.
Limestone pavement: blocks called clints, separated by fissures called grikes.
Turloughs: seasonal lakes in hollows, which fill in winter and drain in summer.
Caves: Aillwee Cave and Doolin Cave, which holds the Great Stalactite, about 7.3 m long.
Mullaghmore: a hill of folded, terraced limestone.
Very few surface rivers, because drainage is underground.
Glaciation: granite erratics from Connemara rest on the limestone, showing that ice scraped off the soil and exposed the pavement.

notes.h: The Burren: plants, land use and tourism
points: Plants from Arctic-alpine and Mediterranean environments grow side by side, for example the spring gentian and mountain avens.
Winterage: cattle graze the upland limestone in winter, because the rock stores heat and the ground is dry.
Poulnabrone, a Neolithic portal tomb (dolmen), stands on the limestone pavement.
Burren National Park protects part of the area near Mullaghmore.
The Burren and Cliffs of Moher UNESCO Global Geopark: tourism is a major activity.

notes.b: South Munster is a region of Old Red Sandstone ridges alternating with Carboniferous limestone valleys.
points: Armorican folding about 300 million years ago, on an east–west trend, produced anticlines and synclines.
Differential erosion left the harder sandstone standing as ridges and wore the limestone down into valleys.
Drowned valleys at the coast form rias: Bantry Bay, Dingle Bay and the Kenmare River.
Ridges (anticlines of sandstone): Macgillycuddy's Reeks, the Galtee Mountains, the Knockmealdown Mountains and the Caha Mountains.
Valleys (synclines of limestone): the Blackwater valley and the Lee valley.
Trellised drainage: rivers flow east along the valleys. The River Blackwater then turns sharply south at Cappoquin, Co. Waterford, and reaches the sea at Youghal. The Lee flows east to Cork Harbour.
Human consequences: towns, routes and fertile farmland lie in the valleys, while the ridges carry rough grazing, forestry and bog.

notes.b: The Northern European Plain is a vast lowland, mostly low, flat or gently rolling, stretching from western France into Russia.
points: Countries crossed: France (north), Belgium, the Netherlands, northern Germany, Denmark and Poland, and into Russia.
Glacial deposits, including moraines, outwash sands and lakes, shape the north of the plain.
A belt of loess, a wind-blown silt, forms fertile soils along the southern edge.
Loess soils support wheat and sugar beet.
The Rhine and Elbe flow north to the North Sea; the Oder and Vistula flow north to the Baltic.
Polders: land reclaimed from the sea in the Netherlands. The Afsluitdijk, completed in 1932, closed off the Zuiderzee.
Human consequences: fertile farmland, easy movement for transport, dense population and major cities, including Berlin, Warsaw, Hamburg and Amsterdam.
The Burren is defined by its rock type, Carboniferous limestone.
Munster ridge and valley is defined by its geological structure, folded sandstone and limestone.
The Northern European Plain is defined by its relief and its surface deposits, glacial and loess.
The Wicklow Mountains and the Leinster batholith are granite uplands, also classed as geomorphological regions; their landforms are taught in geo-rocks-weathering-s4.

keyTerms.definition: An area of the earth's surface that shares one or more criteria which make it different from the areas around it.
The characteristics used to identify and define a region, such as climate, language or wealth.
A band of gradual change between two regions, which replaces a sharp boundary for physical and cultural regions.
A large area with similar temperature, precipitation and seasonal pattern, usually with similar vegetation and soils.
The climate of Ireland and North West Europe: mild winters, cool summers, a small temperature range and rain in every month.
A warm ocean current, the extension of the Gulf Stream, which keeps winters mild in north-western Europe.
Rain caused when moist air is forced up over mountains, cools and releases its moisture.
The drier lee side of mountains, sheltered from prevailing winds, as on Ireland's east.
An area with a distinctive landscape produced by the same rock type, geological structure or landforming processes.
A landscape of limestone shaped by solution, with pavements, caves and few surface rivers.
A clint is a block of limestone pavement; a grike is a fissure separating one clint from the next.
A seasonal lake in a hollow of limestone that fills in winter and drains in summer.
The grazing of cattle on upland limestone in winter, when the rock stores heat and the ground is dry.
An anticline is an upfold of rock layers; a syncline is a downfold.
A drowned river valley on the coast, formed when the sea floods the lower end of a valley.
A wind-blown silt deposit that forms fertile soils, here along the southern edge of the Northern European Plain.
Land reclaimed from the sea and protected from flooding by embankments.

questions.prompt: Using a climatic region you have studied, explain how climate can be used to identify a region.
questions.model: Definition: a climatic region is a large area with similar temperature, precipitation and seasonal pattern, usually with similar vegetation and soils. Take the cool temperate oceanic climate of Ireland. Give the temperature figures (mild winters, cool summers, a small annual range) and the rainfall figures, with rain in every month and no dry season. Explain the controls: latitude, the North Atlantic Drift, the maritime influence, prevailing south-westerly winds, Atlantic depressions and their fronts, and relief rainfall. Describe the variation within Ireland: the wetter west, the rain shadow in the east, the sunnier south-east and the milder coasts. Show how the climate extends across North West Europe and changes eastward into a continental climate with colder winters, warmer summers, a larger range, lower rainfall and a summer maximum, so the boundary is a transition zone. Finish with the links to vegetation (deciduous oak and ash forest, brown earth) and farming (grass for most of the year, supporting cattle and dairying). Do not include geomorphology.

questions.prompt: Describe and explain two geomorphological regions you have studied.
questions.model: Choose the Burren (karst) and Munster ridge and valley. For the Burren: Carboniferous limestone; name the landforms (limestone pavement of clints and grikes, turloughs, caves) and explain that drainage is underground with few surface rivers; explain that glaciation exposed the pavement; describe the plants, winterage grazing, Poulnabrone and the UNESCO Geopark with its tourism. For Munster ridge and valley: east-west folding about 300 million years ago; Old Red Sandstone ridges and Carboniferous limestone valleys, named; the trellised drainage of the Blackwater and the Lee; rias at the coast; human consequences of towns, routes and farmland in the valleys and rough grazing, forestry and bog on the ridges. Give no more formation detail than one bullet per landform.

questions.prompt: Explain what is meant by a region, and give one example of a region at a local scale and one at a continental scale.
questions.model: A region is an area of the earth's surface that shares one or more criteria which make it different from the areas around it. Local scale: Co. Clare (or the Burren). Continental scale: North West Europe.
